case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an employer asserting a Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) exemption must prove the exemption by a preponderance of the evidence or by clear and convincing evidence.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq. (federal minimum wage and overtime requirements and statutory exemptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the ordinary default standard in civil litigation—preponderance of the evidence—governs proof of FLSA exemptions, and that the Fourth Circuit erred by imposing a heightened clear-and-convincing standard not supported by the FLSA’s text, this Court’s general standard-of-proof jurisprudence, or the treatment of exemptions in other circuits; they emphasize that civil monetary disputes presumptively use preponderance and there is no special reason to depart from that baseline for FLSA exemptions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Supreme Court review is not warranted because the standard-of-proof issue is rarely (if ever) outcome-determinative and was not dispositive in this case, minimizing the practical importance of the Fourth Circuit’s rule and suggesting the Court should deny certiorari (or at least not expend resources on plenary review).

John Roberts.reasoning: The Respondent’s strongest point—FLSA’s remedial purpose and under-enforcement concerns—cannot, under our standard-of-proof cases, justify inventing a clear-and-convincing burden absent statutory direction; Addington treats heightened burdens as exceptional and tied to unusually weighty interests, not ordinary wage disputes. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Grogan v. Garner usefully reinforces the institutional premise that preponderance is the civil default even when Congress pursues important remedial policies, and courts should not recalibrate the risk of error by policy preference. Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch correctly note that Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” principle forecloses any atextual thumb-on-the-scale against exemptions, and a heightened evidentiary standard would operate as precisely that. A narrow holding limited to the standard of proof—leaving intact who bears the burden and the substantive exemption elements—best preserves uniformity and institutional legitimacy.

Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Addington properly cabins heightened burdens to exceptional contexts involving liberty, stigma, or comparably weighty interests, which ordinary wage disputes do not present. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Grogan v. Garner reinforces that, absent textual direction, preponderance remains the civil default even when Congress pursues important remedial aims, so the Fourth Circuit’s rule is atextual. Encino Motorcars, as Justice Gorsuch notes, further forecloses any “thumb on the scale” against exemptions via extra-statutory evidentiary hurdles rather than a fair reading of § 213.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the FLSA’s remedial purpose and the old practice of construing exemptions narrowly, but that is not a textual basis for ratcheting up the evidentiary standard; it is exactly the sort of policy-driven “thumb on the scale” Encino Motorcars rejects. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Addington treats clear-and-convincing proof as exceptional—reserved for contexts implicating liberty, stigma, or comparably weighty interests—not routine wage-and-hour disputes. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Grogan v. Garner further confirms that, absent statutory instruction, we default to preponderance even where Congress pursues important remedial aims; courts do not reallocate the risk of error by inventing heightened burdens. The practical consequences also cut against the Fourth Circuit’s rule: it would predictably expand liability and compliance costs beyond what Congress specified in § 213, effectively amending the statute through procedure.

But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Addington reserves clear-and-convincing evidence for extraordinary settings implicating liberty, stigma, or similarly weighty interests, and routine wage-and-hour liability does not fit that category. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Grogan v. Garner further persuades me that, absent statutory direction, we apply the civil default of preponderance rather than reallocating the risk of error by judicial policy preference. Encino Motorcars also cautions against any “thumb on the scale” against exemptions, and a heightened proof standard would function as exactly that even while nominally leaving the substantive exemption elements intact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—remedial purpose plus employer/employee asymmetry warrants clear-and-convincing proof—still asks us to reallocate the risk of error without a statutory hook, and Addington cabins that move to exceptional contexts (liberty, stigma) rather than ordinary wage liability. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is most persuasive to me: absent congressional direction, we apply the civil default, and Grogan confirms that important remedial aims do not themselves justify judicially inventing heightened burdens. Encino Motorcars further undermines any “thumb-on-the-scale” approach against exemptions; a clear-and-convincing standard would effectively narrow § 213 through procedure rather than a fair reading of text. I therefore remain with petitioner: preponderance is textually coherent, administrable, and leaves the employer bearing the burden to prove the exemption.

Chief Justice Roberts is right that Addington v. Texas treats heightened standards as exceptional—typically tied to liberty, stigma, or other unusually weighty interests—and a routine wage-and-hour dispute does not justify reallocating the risk of error by judicial innovation. Justice Kagan’s citation to Grogan v. Garner usefully reinforces that, absent contrary statutory instruction, ordinary civil burdens apply even when important federal policies are at stake. On textualist and separation-of-powers grounds, courts should not effectively rewrite § 213 by inventing extra-statutory evidentiary hurdles.

Justice Kagan’s citation to Grogan reinforces that, absent statutory direction, the default preponderance standard governs even when a party asserts an exception/affirmative defense. Encino Motorcars further undercuts any attempt to smuggle in a “disfavored exemptions” thumb-on-the-scale through evidentiary doctrine rather than interpretation.

Moreover, Encino Motorcars, LLC v. A narrow holding adopting the preponderance standard promotes uniformity and institutional legitimacy while respecting Congress’s chosen balance between overtime requirements and exemptions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FLSA’s text, 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq., nowhere prescribes a clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard for establishing statutory exemptions, so courts should apply the ordinary civil default of proof by a preponderance of the evidence. Texas, 441 U.S. 418, 423 (1979), and nothing about a private monetary dispute over overtime wages warrants the exceptional heightened standard. Imposing clear and convincing evidence effectively amends the statute by judicial fiat and displaces Congress’s chosen scheme, contrary to textualism and the Constitution’s allocation of lawmaking authority. The Fourth Circuit’s heightened standard therefore lacks textual foundation and should be rejected in favor of the default preponderance rule.

Addington v. Texas recognizes that clear-and-convincing evidence is reserved for contexts implicating particularly important interests (there, involuntary commitment), not routine wage-and-hour disputes between private parties. As this Court explained in Herman & McLean v. Huddleston and Halo Electronics v. Pulse Electronics, courts should not impose a heightened standard merely as a policy preference where the statute supplies no basis for it. A clear-and-convincing requirement would improperly tilt the playing field against employers beyond what Congress enacted, with predictable practical consequences for compliance costs and enforcement.

Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979), underscores that clear-and-convincing evidence is an extraordinary standard justified only when especially weighty individual interests are at stake, which is not inherent in an employer’s assertion of an FLSA exemption under 29 U.S.C. § 213. Encino Motorcars, LLC v. While the FLSA’s remedial purpose protects vulnerable workers, that goal is better served by clear, uniform, and administrable standards nationwide than by an atextual heightened burden that invites inconsistency and litigation costs that can impair access to justice on both sides.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an employer must prove the applicability of a Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) exemption by a preponderance of the evidence or by clear and convincing evidence.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), 29 U.S.C. §§ 201 et seq. (including the Act’s minimum wage and overtime requirements and statutory exemptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that FLSA exemptions, like other civil affirmative defenses concerning monetary liability, should be proven by the ordinary civil standard—preponderance of the evidence—and that the Fourth Circuit erred by imposing a heightened clear-and-convincing burden with no textual basis in the FLSA, no support in this Court’s standard-of-proof jurisprudence, and in conflict with other circuits; they contend the Court should at least summarily reverse to restore the default civil evidentiary rule and ensure uniformity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Supreme Court review is unnecessary because the dispute over the evidentiary label is rarely outcome-determinative, was not outcome-determinative on the facts of this case, and has not created meaningful practical problems like forum shopping; they therefore urge denial of certiorari (and defend the judgment below, maintaining that even if the standard were preponderance, the result would not change).
key_precedents: Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979) (discussing standards of proof and noting they may not always change outcomes but reflect societal valuation of interests)

Encino Motorcars, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett emphasize, rejects an atextual thumb on the scale against exemptions and instead requires a “fair reading,” which is incompatible with imposing a heightened persuasion standard. A narrow holding—preponderance governs the employer’s burden of persuasion for FLSA exemptions, without revisiting who bears that burden or other FLSA burden-shifting doctrines—best preserves uniformity and institutional legitimacy.
